SplatFlux: Feed-Forward 4D Gaussian Reconstruction and Generation from Video Latents

Runmin Zhang ††thanks: Equal contribution.††thanks: Internship at Ant Group. Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Binglin Ren11footnotemark: 1 22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Zhu Yu11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Fudong Wang Affiliation: Ant Group    Jiangke Lin Affiliation: Ant Group    Yichun Shentu Affiliation: Ant Group    Si-Yuan Cao Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Yi Yuan ††thanks: Corresponding authors. Affiliation: Ant Group    Hui-Liang Shen33footnotemark: 3 Email: runmin_zhang@zju.edu.cnProject Page: https://rm-zhang.github.io/SplatFlux/ Affiliation: Zhejiang University
Abstract

This work presents SplatFlux, a feed-forward latent-to-4DGS framework for both video-based 4D reconstruction and conditional 4D generation. Our key observation is that observed videos and conditionally generated content can be represented in the same pretrained video latent space, allowing both tasks to be formulated as latent-to-4DGS decoding. To construct compact and temporally coherent 4D scenes, SplatFlux introduces a static-dynamic decoupled 4D Gaussian representation that explicitly predicts dynamic probabilities for Gaussian primitives. This representation separates static scene structures from moving regions, enabling complete 4D scene construction in a feed-forward manner through static aggregation and dynamic motion interpolation. To learn static-dynamic decomposition and dynamic Gaussian motion without costly annotations, we further develop an auxiliary distillation strategy that provides pseudo dynamic masks and optical-flow cues. Extensive experiments across 3D and 4D reconstruction and generation demonstrate that SplatFlux achieves state-of-the-art performance.

1 Introduction

Reconstructing and synthesizing dynamic 3D worlds is essential for filmmaking, VR/AR, and physical AI systems grounded in closed-loop simulation (Bahmani et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025a; Wen et al., 2025). Recent feed-forward geometry and depth models (Wang et al., 2025c; Lin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2025e; Wang et al., 2024) demonstrate that rich 3D information can be inferred directly from visual observations. Building on this progress, feed-forward 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) methods (Xu et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025a; Hur et al., 2026) have emerged to predict temporally coherent Gaussian primitives for efficient dynamic scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis.

Despite this progress, most existing feed-forward 4DGS approaches (Xu et al., 2025b; Lin et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2024; Hur et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025b) are developed for reconstructing dynamic scenes from observed videos. In parallel, modern video generative models (Team, 2024; Kong et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024) can synthesize high-quality video latents from user conditions, providing conditionally generated dynamic visual content in the video latent domain. These advances suggest a latent-domain formulation of 4DGS, where both captured videos and generated content can be represented as video latent sequences before being decoded into dynamic Gaussian representations.

Nevertheless, a key challenge lies in separating and representing static and dynamic components within a complete 4D scene. Existing feed-forward 4DGS approaches often separate static and dynamic components indirectly, through temporal lifespan modeling (Xu et al., 2025b), tracking-based post-processing (Yang et al., 2026), or motion-induced displacement prediction (Lin et al., 2025a). Such implicit formulations may entangle moving objects with static scene structures, especially under complex motion and occlusion.

In this work, we present SplatFlux, a feed-forward latent-to-4DGS framework for both video-based reconstruction and conditional 4D generation. Our key observation is that observed videos and conditionally generated content can be represented in the same pretrained video latent space (Wan et al., 2025). Observed videos are compressed into latent sequences by the VAE encoder, while conditional generation directly produces latent sequences in this space. This common latent representation allows both tasks to be formulated as a unified latent-to-4DGS decoding problem, enabling a shared decoder to map video latents from different sources into dynamic Gaussian representations.

Beyond this task-level unification, SplatFlux further addresses the representation-level ambiguity between static scene structures and moving regions. Instead of inducing static-dynamic separation implicitly from temporal cues, we introduce a static-dynamic decoupled 4D Gaussian representation by explicitly predicting dynamic probabilities for Gaussian primitives. This explicit representation enables complete 4D scene construction in a feed-forward manner without relying on any post-processing. To learn static-dynamic decomposition and dynamic Gaussian motion without costly annotations, we adopt an auxiliary distillation strategy. Specifically, we supervise dynamic probabilities with pseudo dynamic masks generated by vision-language-guided segmentation (Bai et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025), and constrain dynamic Gaussian motion using pseudo optical-flow labels (Zhang et al., 2025c). These complementary signals provide scalable supervision for explicit static-dynamic decomposition and dynamic motion learning.

We evaluate SplatFlux across 3D and 4D reconstruction and generation tasks. Experiments demonstrate that SplatFlux achieves state-of-the-art results. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose SplatFlux, a feed-forward latent-to-4DGS framework that decodes video latents from different sources into 4D Gaussian representations, supporting both video-based 4D reconstruction and conditional 4D generation.

  • •

    We introduce a static-dynamic decoupled 4D Gaussian representation through explicit dynamic probability estimation, enabling compact and complete 4D scene construction in a feed-forward manner.

  • •

    We develop an auxiliary distillation strategy that uses vision-language-guided dynamic masks and optical-flow cues to learn static-dynamic decomposition and dynamic Gaussian motion without costly annotations.

  • •

    Extensive experiments across 3D and 4D reconstruction and generation tasks demonstrate that SplatFlux achieves state-of-the-art performance.

2 Related Work

2.1 3D/4D Reconstruction and Novel View Synthesis

Traditional approaches typically rely on costly per-scene optimization, including classical structure-from-motion (SfM) (Schonberger and Frahm, 2016), neural radiance fields (NeRF) (Mildenhall et al., 2020), and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023). Several methods (Wang et al., 2025d; Sun et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2026b; Lei et al., 2025) further extend 3DGS to dynamic scenes through temporal deformation modeling and additional supervision estimated from vision foundation models. With the growth of large-scale 3D datasets and foundation models (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020; Oquab et al., 2023; Siméoni et al., 2025; Ranftl et al., 2021), feed-forward 3D and 4D reconstruction approaches (Wang et al., 2024; Leroy et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025f; Wang et al., 2026c; Lin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025c; Fang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025e; Chen et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025b; Hu et al., 2025b; Wen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Yu et al., 2026a) have become increasingly prominent. Methods such as DUSt3R (Wang et al., 2024) and VGGT (Wang et al., 2025c) directly predict dense geometry and camera parameters from images, while approaches (Ye et al., 2025a; Ye et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b) like AnySplat (Jiang et al., 2025) predict 3D Gaussian primitives for novel view synthesis in static scenes.

For feed-forward dynamic novel view synthesis, recent methods such as L4GM (Ren et al., 2024), STORM (Yang et al., 2025a), 4DGT (Xu et al., 2025b), MoVieS (Lin et al., 2025a), DGS-LRM (Lin et al., 2025b), and BTimer (Liang et al., 2024) estimate motion-related attributes for Gaussian primitives. However, most of these approaches still assume posed inputs, and MoVieS (Lin et al., 2025a) and BTimer (Liang et al., 2024) further require additional network inference for rendering at each target timestamp. UFO-4D (Hur et al., 2026) relaxes the pose requirement, but is limited to two input views. NeoVerse (Yang et al., 2026) supports unposed video inputs, yet relies on hand-crafted global motion tracking to aggregate a scene-level representation. These limitations highlight the need for a feed-forward framework that can infer a complete dynamic Gaussian representation from unposed monocular videos, without per-timestamp network inference or hand-crafted post-processing.

2.2 3D/4D Generation

Recent 3D and 4D generative approaches have made notable progress by distilling or fine-tuning pretrained image and video diffusion models (Saharia et al., 2022; Rombach et al., 2022; Wan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024). The pioneering work DreamFusion (Poole et al., 2022) introduces score distillation sampling (SDS) to optimize 3D representations by distilling gradients from pretrained diffusion models. Subsequent methods (Wang et al., 2023; Singer et al., 2023; Bahmani et al., 2024a; Bahmani et al., 2024b) improve the distillation objective or extend this paradigm to 4D scene generation.

Another line of work (Tang et al., 2024; Szymanowicz et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024a; Go et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025b; Cai et al., 2025) combines generative diffusion priors with 3D reconstruction for efficient 3D scene generation. Approaches such as CAT3D (Gao et al., 2024) and SEVA (Zhou et al., 2025a) first synthesize multi-view images with diffusion models, followed by 3D reconstruction. In contrast, other methods (Yang et al., 2025b; Cai et al., 2025; Go et al., 2025b; Go et al., 2025a) bypass explicit RGB multi-view synthesis, and directly decode latent features into 3D Gaussian primitives. To support 4D content generation, some approaches (Wang et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2024) generate synchronized multi-view videos, while others extend video generation to dynamic point maps (Zhu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025c; Park et al., 2025). Recent methods such as Lyra (Bahmani et al., 2026) and Diff4Splat (Pan et al., 2025) further explore dynamic Gaussian generation. However, they rely on target-time Gaussian prediction mechanisms, as in BTimer (Liang et al., 2024) and MoVieS (Lin et al., 2025a), where rendering a new timestamp requires additional network inference to obtain the corresponding Gaussian state. In contrast, SplatFlux formulates conditional 4D generation as latent-to-4DGS decoding, and directly produces a complete 4DGS representation that supports continuous-time rendering without per-timestamp network inference.

3 Method

3.1 Overview

We introduce SplatFlux, a fully feed-forward framework that unifies 4D Gaussian reconstruction and generation under a latent-to-4DGS formulation. Given a latent sequence 𝐳0:T−1\mathbf{z}_{0:T-1}11 1 We use the pretrained Wan VAE latent space (Wan et al., 2025) as the common latent domain for both tasks. obtained by encoding observed videos or by conditional generation, SplatFlux decodes it into a 4D Gaussian scene 𝒮\mathcal{S}:

𝒮=𝒟GS(𝐳0:T−1),\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{GS}}(\mathbf{z}_{0:T-1}), (1)

where 𝒟GS\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{GS}} is the shared 4DGS decoder. At the core of SplatFlux is a static-dynamic decoupled 4D Gaussian representation. Each Gaussian primitive is assigned a dynamic probability for explicit static-dynamic decomposition. Static Gaussians are aggregated across frames into a compact scene representation, while dynamic Gaussians remain frame-anchored and are propagated by local velocities for continuous-time rendering. This allows SplatFlux to construct a complete 4D Gaussian scene for arbitrary-view and arbitrary-time rendering without hand-crafted post-processing or per-timestamp network inference. Fig. 2 illustrates the overall pipeline.

3.2 Decoupled 4D Gaussian Representation

Per-frame 4DGS Representation. Given a latent sequence 𝐳0:T−1\mathbf{z}_{0:T-1}, our decoder predicts a set of per-pixel 4D Gaussian primitives for each timestamp. We denote the 4D Gaussians at frame tt as

𝒢t={gt,i=(𝝁t,i,𝐬t,i,𝐪t,i,αt,i,𝐜t,i,mt,i,𝐯t,i+,𝐯t,i−)}i=1H​W,\mathcal{G}_{t}=\left\{g_{t,i}=\left(\bm{\mu}_{t,i},\mathbf{s}_{t,i},\mathbf{q}_{t,i},\alpha_{t,i},\mathbf{c}_{t,i},m_{t,i},\mathbf{v}^{+}_{t,i},\mathbf{v}^{-}_{t,i}\right)\right\}_{i=1}^{HW}, (2)

where ii indexes the image grid, and HH and WW denote the output resolution. Each primitive gt,ig_{t,i} is parameterized by its 3D center 𝝁t,i\bm{\mu}_{t,i}, scale 𝐬t,i\mathbf{s}_{t,i}, rotation 𝐪t,i\mathbf{q}_{t,i}, opacity αt,i\alpha_{t,i}, color 𝐜t,i\mathbf{c}_{t,i}, dynamic probability mt,im_{t,i}, forward velocity 𝐯t,i+\mathbf{v}^{+}_{t,i}, and backward velocity 𝐯t,i−\mathbf{v}^{-}_{t,i}. We note that the dynamic probability enables explicit static-dynamic decomposition of Gaussian primitives in a feed-forward manner, while 𝐯t,i+\mathbf{v}^{+}_{t,i} and 𝐯t,i−\mathbf{v}^{-}_{t,i} support arbitrary-time rendering by locally interpolating Gaussian motion without per-timestamp network inference.

Complete Scene Reconstruction. To obtain a compact and complete 4DGS scene, we do not simply concatenate per-frame Gaussians across timestamps, as this would introduce substantial redundancy in static regions and entangle static and dynamic content. Instead, we explicitly separate the predicted Gaussians according to their dynamic probabilities. Given a threshold τm\tau_{m}, the Gaussians at frame tt are divided into static and dynamic subsets as

𝒢ts={gt,i∣mt,i<τm},𝒢td={gt,i∣mt,i≥τm}.\mathcal{G}^{s}_{t}=\{g_{t,i}\mid m_{t,i}<\tau_{m}\},\quad\mathcal{G}^{d}_{t}=\{g_{t,i}\mid m_{t,i}\geq\tau_{m}\}. (3)

For static regions, we perform multi-frame aggregation through differentiable voxelization (Jiang et al., 2025) to merge redundant primitives, obtaining 𝒢s=Agg⁡(⋃t=0T−1𝒢ts)\mathcal{G}^{s}=\mathrm{Agg}\left(\bigcup_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathcal{G}^{s}_{t}\right). The complete 4DGS scene is therefore composed as 𝒮=𝒢s∪{𝒢td}t=0T−1\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{G}^{s}\cup\left\{\mathcal{G}^{d}_{t}\right\}_{t=0}^{T-1}, where 𝒢s\mathcal{G}^{s} represents the compact static scene, and {𝒢td}\{\mathcal{G}^{d}_{t}\} preserves dynamic regions with their associated velocities for continuous-time rendering. Fig. 2(c) illustrates the process of our complete scene reconstruction.

For an arbitrary target time ttargett_{\mathrm{target}} between two adjacent timestamps tt and t+1t+1, we move the dynamic Gaussians 𝒢td\mathcal{G}^{d}_{t} and 𝒢t+1d\mathcal{G}^{d}_{t+1} to ttargett_{\mathrm{target}} using linear motion interpolation (Hur et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025b) as

𝝁t→ttarget,i=𝝁t,i+(ttarget−t)​𝐯t,i+,𝝁t+1→ttarget,i=𝝁t+1,i+(t+1−ttarget)​𝐯t+1,i−.\bm{\mu}_{t\rightarrow t_{\mathrm{target}},i}=\bm{\mu}_{t,i}+(t_{\mathrm{target}}-t)\mathbf{v}^{+}_{t,i},\quad\bm{\mu}_{t+1\rightarrow t_{\mathrm{target}},i}=\bm{\mu}_{t+1,i}+(t+1-t_{\mathrm{target}})\mathbf{v}^{-}_{t+1,i}. (4)

The scene at ttargett_{\mathrm{target}} is then composed of the static Gaussians and moved dynamic Gaussians, enabling rasterization (Kerbl et al., 2023) of novel views. Overall, this static-dynamic decoupled representation provides a compact and complete 4D scene by aggregating static structures across frames while preserving dynamic regions with local motion for continuous-time rendering.

3.3 Unified Latent-to-4DGS Decoding

Reconstruction from Videos. Given a monocular video sequence 𝐈0:T−1={I0,…,IT−1}\mathbf{I}_{0:T-1}=\{I_{0},\ldots,I_{T-1}\}, we use the frozen Wan VAE encoder ℰ\mathcal{E} to extract latents as 𝐳t=ℰ⁡(It)\mathbf{z}_{t}=\mathcal{E}(I_{t}). We note that each frame is treated as an individual image and encoded independently, without applying temporal compression in the video VAE encoder. This frame-wise design avoids temporal compression, and allows training with unordered multi-view image datasets.

Generation from Conditions. For input conditions cc, such as a text prompt, a single image, or their combination, we use a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) (Peebles and Xie, 2023) as the generator Φgen\Phi_{\mathrm{gen}} to produce a latent sequence as 𝐳0:T−1=Φgen(c)\mathbf{z}_{0:T-1}=\Phi_{\mathrm{gen}}(c). Different from standard video generation pipelines that decode generated latents into RGB videos, we directly decode the generated latent sequence into a 4DGS scene using our proposed decoder 𝒟GS\mathcal{D}_{\textrm{GS}}.

Architecture of 4DGS Decoder. As shown in Fig. 2(b), the decoder first maps the low-dimensional VAE latent sequence into high-dimensional feature tokens through a latent projector. The resulting tokens are then processed by alternating attention blocks (Wang et al., 2025c) to exchange spatial and temporal information. Finally, we use three prediction heads (Ranftl et al., 2021) to estimate geometry, appearance, and motion attributes from the spatiotemporal fused features 𝐅t\mathbf{F}_{t} as

(𝐝t,𝐫t)=ℋgeo​(𝐅t),𝐚t=ℋapp​(𝐅t),(𝐦t,𝐯t+,𝐯t−)=ℋmotion​(𝐅t),(\mathbf{d}_{t},\mathbf{r}_{t})=\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{geo}}(\mathbf{F}_{t}),\quad\mathbf{a}_{t}=\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{app}}(\mathbf{F}_{t}),\quad(\mathbf{m}_{t},\mathbf{v}^{+}_{t},\mathbf{v}^{-}_{t})=\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{motion}}(\mathbf{F}_{t}), (5)

where 𝐝t\mathbf{d}_{t} and 𝐫t\mathbf{r}_{t} denote depth and ray map (Lin et al., 2026), 𝐚t\mathbf{a}_{t} denotes appearance attributes including scale, rotation, opacity, and color, and 𝐦t\mathbf{m}_{t}, 𝐯t+\mathbf{v}^{+}_{t}, and 𝐯t−\mathbf{v}^{-}_{t} denote the dynamic mask, forward velocity, and backward velocity, respectively. The Gaussian centers are then derived from the predicted 𝐝t\mathbf{d}_{t} and 𝐫t\mathbf{r}_{t}.

3.4 Model Training

Learning static-dynamic decomposition and dynamic Gaussian motion would benefit from direct supervision with dynamic masks and motion labels. However, such annotations are costly to obtain, and are typically limited to small-scale synthetic datasets (Karaev et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023). Relying only on rendering losses provides weak constraints on dynamic probabilities and local velocities, often leading to ambiguous decomposition and inaccurate motion estimation.

To address this issue, we adopt an auxiliary distillation strategy. We generate pseudo dynamic masks and optical-flow labels using expert foundation models (Bai et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025c), and use them as auxiliary supervision during training. This provides scalable guidance on where the scene should be decomposed and how dynamic Gaussians should move, allowing SplatFlux to benefit from large-scale training without costly annotations.

Dynamic mask supervision. To construct pseudo labels for dynamic masks, we first use Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) to detect dynamic objects in videos, and generate a text description including the category and visual attributes for each detected dynamic object. We then use this description as the prompt for Sa2VA (Yuan et al., 2025) to segment the corresponding object. The masks of all detected dynamic objects in the same image are merged into a pseudo dynamic mask.

Given the predicted dynamic mask 𝐦t\mathbf{m}_{t} and its pseudo label 𝐦~t\widetilde{\mathbf{m}}_{t}, we compute the dynamic mask loss as a combination of binary cross-entropy, Dice, and binarization regularization:

ℒdyn=ℒBCE​(𝐦t,𝐦~t)+λDice​ℒDice​(𝐦t,𝐦~t)+λbin​ℒbin​(𝐦t),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BCE}}(\mathbf{m}_{t},\widetilde{\mathbf{m}}_{t})+\lambda_{\mathrm{Dice}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Dice}}(\mathbf{m}_{t},\widetilde{\mathbf{m}}_{t})+\lambda_{\mathrm{bin}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bin}}(\mathbf{m}_{t}), (6)

where the binarization regularization is defined as

ℒbin​(𝐦t)=1|Ω|​∑𝐱∈Ω𝐦t​(𝐱)​(1−𝐦t​(𝐱)),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bin}}(\mathbf{m}_{t})=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega}\mathbf{m}_{t}(\mathbf{x})\left(1-\mathbf{m}_{t}(\mathbf{x})\right), (7)

and Ω\Omega denotes all image pixels. The dynamic mask supervision provides an explicit signal for separating static and dynamic Gaussians, which is essential for feed-forward 4D scene construction.

Motion supervision. To supervise local velocities, we employ the optical-flow foundation model UFM (Zhang et al., 2025c) to generate pseudo motion cues. Instead of directly supervising velocities in 3D space, we project the predicted Gaussian motion into the image plane, and minimize the discrepancy between the optical flow induced by the predicted Gaussian motion and the pseudo flow labels from UFM.

Given the predicted depth 𝐝t\mathbf{d}_{t}, ray map 𝐫t\mathbf{r}_{t}, and bidirectional velocities 𝐯t+\mathbf{v}^{+}_{t} and 𝐯t−\mathbf{v}^{-}_{t}, we compute the Gaussian center at pixel 𝐱∈Ω\mathbf{x}\in\Omega as 𝝁t​(𝐱)=𝒫⁡(𝐱,𝐝t​(𝐱),𝐫t​(𝐱))\bm{\mu}_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{P}\bigl(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{d}_{t}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{r}_{t}(\mathbf{x})\bigr), where 𝒫⁡(⋅)\mathcal{P}(\cdot) denotes the backward projection function. The optical flows from frame tt to t+1t+1 and t−1t-1 can be derived as

𝐅t→t+1​(𝐱)=Πt+1​(𝝁t​(𝐱)+𝐯t+​(𝐱))−𝐱,\mathbf{F}_{t\rightarrow t+1}(\mathbf{x})=\Pi_{t+1}\left(\bm{\mu}_{t}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{v}^{+}_{t}(\mathbf{x})\right)-\mathbf{x}, (8)
𝐅t→t−1​(𝐱)=Πt−1​(𝝁t​(𝐱)+𝐯t−​(𝐱))−𝐱.\mathbf{F}_{t\rightarrow t-1}(\mathbf{x})=\Pi_{t-1}\left(\bm{\mu}_{t}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{v}^{-}_{t}(\mathbf{x})\right)-\mathbf{x}. (9)

Here, Πt+1​(⋅)\Pi_{t+1}(\cdot) and Πt−1​(⋅)\Pi_{t-1}(\cdot) denote the projection functions using the corresponding ray maps. Let 𝐅~t→t+1\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t\rightarrow t+1} and 𝐅~t→t−1\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t\rightarrow t-1} denote the pseudo optical flows estimated by the teacher model. We supervise the optical flows induced by Gaussian motion as

ℒflow=1|Ω|​∑𝐱∈Ωwt​(𝐱)​(‖𝐅t→t+1​(𝐱)−𝐅~t→t+1​(𝐱)‖1+‖𝐅t→t−1​(𝐱)−𝐅~t→t−1​(𝐱)‖1),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flow}}=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega}w_{t}(\mathbf{x})\left(\left\|\mathbf{F}_{t\rightarrow t+1}(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t\rightarrow t+1}(\mathbf{x})\right\|_{1}+\left\|\mathbf{F}_{t\rightarrow t-1}(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t\rightarrow t-1}(\mathbf{x})\right\|_{1}\right), (10)

where wt​(𝐱)w_{t}(\mathbf{x}) is a dynamic-region weight derived from the pseudo dynamic mask 𝐦~t\widetilde{\mathbf{m}}_{t}. This weighting encourages the model to focus more on regions with meaningful object motion.

Overall objective. The overall training objective combines geometry, rendering, dynamic mask, and optical-flow losses as

ℒ=λgeo​ℒgeo+λrend​ℒrend+λdyn​ℒdyn+λflow​ℒflow.\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{\mathrm{geo}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{rend}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rend}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{dyn}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{flow}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flow}}. (11)

Here, ℒgeo\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}} supervises the depths and ray maps of source views following the implementation of DA3 (Lin et al., 2026). The rendering loss ℒrend\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rend}} is applied to the rendered RGB images and depths of both source and target views. Specifically, we use ℓ2\ell_{2} and LPIPS (Johnson et al., 2016) losses for RGB rendering, and ℓ1\ell_{1} loss for depth rendering. The dynamic mask loss ℒdyn\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}} provides direct supervision for static-dynamic decomposition, while the optical-flow loss ℒflow\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flow}} constrains the motion of dynamic Gaussians.

Implementation Details. We train SplatFlux on 17 public datasets, covering static and dynamic content across object-centric, indoor, and outdoor scenarios. For the 4DGS decoder, we initialize the alternating attention blocks and geometry head from DA3-Giant (Lin et al., 2026), use the frozen Wan2.1 VAE (Wan et al., 2025) as the latent encoder, and adopt gsplat (Ye et al., 2025b) for differentiable rasterization. For each training iteration, we sample TT source frames and T−1T-1 intermediate target frames between adjacent source frames. The 4DGS decoder is supervised using the objective in Eq. 11. For conditional generation, we fine-tune Wan2.1-14B (Wan et al., 2025) with the standard flow-matching objective, where training videos are encoded into per-frame latent sequences without temporal compression. The generated conditional latents are directly decoded by the shared 4DGS decoder 𝒟GS\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{GS}}. The full training pipeline takes approximately 10 days on 32 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. Details of the training datasets and implementation are provided in Appendix A and Appendix B, respectively.

4 Experiments

4.1 Dynamic Novel View Synthesis

We evaluate SplatFlux for dynamic novel view synthesis on the NVIDIA Dynamic Scene (Yoon et al., 2020), DyCheck (Gao et al., 2022), and DAVIS (Perazzi et al., 2016) datasets. We compare with three state-of-the-art open-sourced approaches (Xu et al., 2025b; Lin et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2026), and list the results in Table 1. The results demonstrate that SplatFlux achieves superior dynamic novel view synthesis without relying on camera poses as input. The qualitative comparison in Fig. 3 further shows that our method produces clearer details with fewer rendering artifacts. In contrast, the comparison approaches often suffer from ghosting artifacts in dynamic regions, or exhibit limited generalization ability on in-the-wild scenes. The detailed evaluation protocol can be found in Appendix B.

4.2 Conditional 3D and 4D Generation

Text-to-3D Generation. We evaluate SplatFlux for text-to-3D generation on SceneBench (Yang et al., 2025b). In alignment with VIST3A (Go et al., 2025a), we employ imaging quality and aesthetic quality in VBench (Huang et al., 2024) for visual fidelity, CLIP Score (Hessel et al., 2021) for text alignment, and alignment, coherence, and style scores in UnifiedReward (Wang et al., 2025g) for overall generation quality. As shown in Table 2, SplatFlux consistently outperforms competing methods across all metrics. Qualitative results in Fig. 4(a) further show that SplatFlux generates scenes that more faithfully match the input text conditions.

Text-to-4D Generation. Following prior work (Park et al., 2025), we evaluate text-to-4D generation on the PenguinVideoBenchmark (Kong et al., 2024). We report VBench (Huang et al., 2024) metrics for quantitative comparison. As shown in Table 3, SplatFlux achieves substantial improvements in both scene consistency and image aesthetics. The qualitative results in Fig. 4(b) further show that our method generates 4D content that better follows the input conditions and exhibits plausible motion. Moreover, we note that SplatFlux produces 4D Gaussian scenes that support photorealistic rendering, whereas baselines are limited to generating dynamic point clouds.

Image-to-4D Generation. In alignment with Park et al. (2025), we evaluate image-to-4D generation on 355 samples from VBench-I2V (Huang et al., 2024). As shown in Table 4, SplatFlux achieves stronger motion dynamics and better perceptual quality in the generated 4D scenes. The qualitative results in Fig. 4(c) further show that SplatFlux generates large-range and physically plausible scene dynamics, whereas the compared methods are mostly limited to relatively local 4D motion.

4.3 Ablations

We present ablation studies on our static-dynamic decoupled representation and auxiliary supervision using the NVIDIA Dynamic Scene dataset in Table 5. Removing the decoupled representation causes the largest performance drop, suggesting that explicit static-dynamic separation is essential for complete 4D scene construction. Without this constraint, the model tends to learn an interpolation-like representation from monocular videos, where static structures may be treated as dynamic, leading to incomplete geometry and holes under novel view rendering, as illustrated in Fig. 5. The two supervision signals further provide complementary constraints for dynamic attributes. Dynamic mask supervision guides where the scene should be decomposed, while optical-flow supervision constrains how dynamic Gaussians should move. Removing either supervision signal degrades performance. Notably, our method does not require perfectly precise pseudo labels, benefiting from the consistency constraints provided by rendering supervision, as shown in Fig. 7.

Please refer to Appendices C and D for more detailed quantitative and qualitative results, including results on video depth estimation, static novel view synthesis, and dynamic object segmentation.

5 Conclusions

We have presented SplatFlux, a unified feed-forward latent-to-4DGS framework for video-based 4D reconstruction and conditional 4D generation. By decoding video latents from different sources into a 4D Gaussian representation, SplatFlux provides a shared formulation for captured and generated dynamic content. We further introduce a static-dynamic decoupled 4D Gaussian representation that supports complete 4D scene construction in a feed-forward manner. Through auxiliary distillation from vision-language-guided dynamic masks and optical-flow cues, SplatFlux learns dynamic attributes without costly annotations. Extensive experiments on 3D and 4D reconstruction and generation demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of SplatFlux.

Appendix

Appendix A Datasets

Table 6 summarizes the 17 datasets used for training SplatFlux. We mainly follow CUT3R (Wang et al., 2025e) for data preprocessing and filtering. For large-scale datasets such as Aria Synthetic Environments (Pan et al., 2023) and Lyra (Bahmani et al., 2026), we select 5000 scenes for efficient training. For datasets with provided dynamic masks, such as OmniWorld-Game (Zhou et al., 2025b) and Dynamic Replica (Karaev et al., 2023), we directly use the masks provided in the dataset. For the remaining dynamic datasets, such as Lyra (Bahmani et al., 2026) and Stereo4D (Jin et al., 2025), we generate pseudo dynamic masks using Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) and Sa2VA (Yuan et al., 2025). During training, we use UFM (Zhang et al., 2025c) to compute pseudo optical-flow supervision for all dynamic datasets. All 17 datasets are used to train the 4DGS decoder, while the generator is trained on DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024), OmniWorld-Game (Zhou et al., 2025b), Stereo4D (Jin et al., 2025), and Lyra (Bahmani et al., 2026).

Appendix B More Implementation Details

Training of the 4DGS Decoder. To improve generalization, we randomly sample the aspect ratio from 0.50.5 to 2.02.0, and resize and crop images while keeping the total number of pixels between 100,000100{,}000 and 250,000250{,}000. The number of source frames TT is randomly sampled from 22 to 1212. We train the 4DGS decoder in two stages. In the first stage, we disable voxelization-based aggregation and train the decoder for 100100K iterations. In the second stage, we enable voxelization-based aggregation to reduce redundant static Gaussians and fine-tune the model for another 5050K iterations. We use the AdamW optimizer with a cosine learning rate schedule and linear warm-up. The maximum learning rates of the two stages are set to 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} and 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, respectively. For the parameters initialized from DA3-Giant (Lin et al., 2026), we scale the learning rate by 0.10.1.

Training of the DiT Generator. We train the DiT generator to produce key frame latent sequences. The generator is fine-tuned for 20,00020{,}000 iterations using LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), with rank r=32r=32, scaling factor α=64\alpha=64, and group size G=64G=64. We optimize the LoRA parameters with AdamW using a learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} and a weight decay of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}.

Evaluation Protocol for dynamic novel view synthesis. For NVIDIA Dynamic Scene, we select 12 input frames in a round-robin manner across cameras, and test on 12 frames from camera 0. For DyCheck, we sample 64 consecutive timestamps for each scene. We reconstruct from 32 frames sampled every two timestamps from a casually captured video (camera 0), and evaluate on all 64 frames from a fixed-camera video (camera 1) together with the remaining 32 frames from camera 0. For DAVIS, we select 60 scenes for evaluation. For each scene, we sample 48 consecutive frames and split them evenly into 24 input frames and 24 evaluation frames. The image resolutions for NVIDIA Dynamic Scene, DyCheck, and DAVIS are set to 560×336560\times 336, 336×448336\times 448, and 560×336560\times 336, respectively.

Appendix C More Comparison Results

In this section, we evaluate SplatFlux on additional tasks, including video depth estimation, static novel view synthesis, and dynamic object segmentation.

C.1 Video Depth Estimation

We evaluate the video depth estimation capability of SplatFlux on the Sintel (Butler et al., 2012), Bonn (Palazzolo et al., 2019), and KITTI (Geiger et al., 2013) datasets. In line with Yu et al. (2026a), the predicted depth sequences are aligned to the ground-truth depth using a scale factor per sequence. Table 7 reports the absolute relative error (Abs Rel) and threshold accuracy (δ1\delta_{1}). SplatFlux achieves competitive performance, outperforming 3D reconstruction foundation models such as VGGT (Wang et al., 2025c) and DA3 (Lin et al., 2026).

C.2 Static Novel View Synthesis

SplatFlux also supports 3D Gaussian reconstruction and rendering of static scenes. We evaluate SplatFlux on the DL3DV-140 benchmark (Ling et al., 2024), and report the comparative results in Table 8. SplatFlux achieves strong overall performance, demonstrating its generalization to static novel view synthesis.

C.3 Dynamic Object Segmentation

We evaluate SplatFlux for dynamic object segmentation on the DAVIS (Perazzi et al., 2016) dataset. Quantitative metrics including mean IoU (JM), recall of IoU (JR), mean contour accuracy (FM), and recall of contour accuracy (FR) are reported in Table 9. SplatFlux achieves the best performance across these metrics, demonstrating its ability to distinguish dynamic regions from static scene content. Qualitative results in Fig. 6 further show that our method produces more accurate and complete dynamic masks.

Appendix D More Qualitative Results

Visualization of the Dynamic Mask. Fig. 7 presents a qualitative comparison between the pseudo dynamic mask used for supervision and the dynamic mask predicted by SplatFlux. Compared with the pseudo mask, SplatFlux produces cleaner dynamic regions and avoids incorrectly classifying static scene structures as dynamic, indicating that the learned static-dynamic decomposition is more robust than the noisy supervision.

Visualization of Reconstructed 4DGS Scenes. Fig. 8 presents additional reconstruction results from SplatFlux, demonstrating independent control of camera pose and time through fixed-camera, frozen-time, and joint camera-time rendering. The rendered sequences preserve scene appearance and motion, exhibiting visual consistency across changes in viewpoint and time.

Visualization of Generated 4DGS Scenes. Fig. 9 presents additional generation results from SplatFlux under text and image conditions. The generated scenes reflect the conditioning content and maintain visual consistency across changes in viewpoint and time.

Appendix E Limitations

SplatFlux currently works in an offline setting and does not support streaming reconstruction or generation. We leave streaming latent decoding to future work.
